newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy reels from stinging EMU slap.
newsitem.headline: Italy reels from stinging EMU slap.

text.p: Italy reeled on Thursday after Brussels dealt a stinging blow to its credibility by consigning it to the EMU second division with Greece.

The European Commission forecast on Wednesday that Italy's 1997 deficit would be 3.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- outside the three percent ceiling set by the Maastricht Treaty to join a single currency at its planned 1999 start.
"Europe's slap" screamed the headline in La Repubblica as the centre-left government accused Brussels of unfairness for forecasting that it was lagging behind on a key deficit goal.
But European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said there was no point playing the victim and Italy should reform its unruly politics to be taken seriously in Europe.
"No-one doubts Italy's goodwill," he told La Repubblica in an interview from Brussels.
"We recognise the efforts of (Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio) Ciampi, but the Italian state is still too slow...
"If these efforts are regularly blocked by parliament, then the Italian system isn't working. It's a system that never manages to keep its promises," Van Miert said.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi has prescribed gallons of bitter budgetary medicine, including deficit-cutting measures totalling some 78 trillion lire ($46 billion) over the past four months in a bid to ensure Italy cannot be faulted on financial grounds.
But Italy fears plans are afoot to keep it out because of a history of chronic political and budgetary instability.

Ciampi slammed the Commission's "total lack of balance", saying it had used far stricter methodology in its analysis of Italy's accounts than that applied to France or Spain. He said the Commission had taken no notice of Italy's strenuous efforts.
Even President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro joined the chorus of complaint. "As a politician, I don't accept that the evaluation should be purely economic," he said during a trip to Germany.
"The political world must rebel against an accountant's view which makes no sense."
Italy's wounded pride stems largely from the fact that heavyweights France and Germany, once seen as EMU certainties, have also been struggling to meet the strict criteria.
"Italy, in the final analysis, will not be judged on quantative criteria but on qualitative ones," Sergio Romano, a former diplomat and respected commentator, wrote in La Stampa.

He agreed with Van Miert that Italy could do far more to help itself. "What has Prodi's government done to reassure its partners? What has it done to deserve a different judgment to yesterday's? Little or nothing," Romano wrote.
He said Italy had failed to implement structural changes to keep spending under lasting control and that despite promises to reform a bloated pension system, nothing had been done.
Van Miert said it was the same story with Italy's stop-start privatisation programme -- "prevarication, wasted time".
Prodi faces battles on both reform of the welfare state and privatisation from the hard-left Communist Refoundation party whose support he needs for a parliamentary majority.
Refoundation, which recently humiliated the government by refusing to back the deployment of a security mission for Albania, has obstructed progress on both subjects so far.
